stories.summary: DaVinci Resolve is today one of the big three editing programs, and its free version offers state-of-the-art editing and colour grading on any laptop. Back in 2010, when it did only colour grading, it cost $800,000. Not a single copy existed in India. Bollywood films were sent to Hollywood for colour grading and shipped back, and that cost was built into the film's budget. Amit learned this from a YouTube video and could hardly believe it.
stories.insight: In less than a generation, tools that only studios could rent have become free downloads. Ajay framed this with a Marxist joke: producers now own the means of production. Two hosts with consumer-grade gear can make what once needed a media company.
stories.quote: There wasn't one in India because it cost eight hundred thousand dollars for color grading.

stories.topic: The Russian Military: Parades Hid the Rot
stories.summary: To illustrate secrecy, the fourth dimension of policy complexity, Ajay pointed to the military. It is widely admired, but it operates under secrecy that can cover a great deal of state failure. Once Putin's war began and the shooting started, the world saw mind-blowing failures inside the Russian military that pompous parades, nationalism and militarism had kept hidden.
stories.insight: Secrecy removes the checks and balances that come from people noticing misbehaviour. Wherever the state works out of sight, assume capability is weaker than the spectacle suggests.
stories.quote: So while there is a lot of admiration and respect for the military, it is also the case that the military is shrouded in secrecy. And that's likely to be the cover for a lot of state failure.

stories.summary: Amit drew on his Seen and the Unseen episodes with Pranay Kotasthane on centrally sponsored schemes and with RS Nilakantan on South India. Kerala's health problem is diabetes and obesity. Bihar and other parts of North and central India struggle with malnourishment. Yet centrally sponsored schemes are designed in Delhi around northern problems and imposed everywhere, without understanding local needs.
stories.insight: One template from the centre cannot fit a country whose regions face opposite problems. This is the practical case for pushing decisions down to the level that knows the problem, which Ajay then named as the subsidiarity principle.
stories.quote: The needs of the North and the South are so different. But the priorities of the North dictate public policy.

stories.topic: How European States Learned to Be States
stories.summary: The Swedish state did not appear fully formed. For three centuries (the 17th, 18th and 19th), European states did essentially two things: run a fiscal system to raise taxes, and wage war, along with the arms, technology and contracting around it. Doing those narrow tasks taught them HR, contracting, checks and balances, corruption control, solving principal-agent problems, and keeping the fauji guys in their barracks. Only then could that hard-won capability be applied to new problems such as vaccines.
stories.insight: State capability is learned by doing a few things for a long time. For India, Ajay argues, the right move is a narrow scope for 25 to 50 years, mastering basics like the police and the judiciary, before arguing over more or less welfare.
stories.quote: It took hundreds of years, but around that, they learned how to be a state.

recommendations.item: Seeing Like a State: How Certain Schemes to Improve the Human Condition Have Failed
recommendations.creator: James C Scott
recommendations.context: Ajay's recommendation in the closing chapter.
recommendations.reason: A reflection on how hard it is for institutions and bureaucracies to see, and on how, when the state does see people, it often inflicts cruelty and violence on them. It takes a sceptical look at making society more legible to the state. That is why Kelkar and Ajay use the phrase 'premature state legibility' in India's digital debates. Ajay calls it a great cautionary book on the fraught relationship between the individual and the state.

recommendations.item: Cicada
recommendations.creator: Shaun Tan
recommendations.context: Amit's recommendation in the closing chapter. It was first recommended to him on a Seen and the Unseen episode on motherhood, and the copy he held up was borrowed from his editor Nomsita.
recommendations.reason: Amit deliberately says nothing about its contents. He calls Shaun Tan a great illustrator, writer and artist, and the book simply 'a marvelous book'.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Praised right after Ajay laid out the four kinds of market failure, and again before the closing recommendations.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a masterpiece. It is the source of the toolkit in this episode: market failure, the complexity test for interventions, and choosing the least intrusive intervention.

recommendations.item: The Art and Science of Economic Policy (Episode 154 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Mentioned alongside In Service of the Republic. Amit notes he has recorded with 'both eminences'.
recommendations.reason: A long conversation with both authors about the framework this episode only sketches.

recommendations.item: Solutions When the Solution is the Problem: Arraying the Disarray in Development
recommendations.creator: Lant Pritchett and Michael Woolcock
recommendations.context: Cited as the 2004 paper behind the first two dimensions of Ajay's test for how hard a policy intervention will be.
recommendations.reason: It proposed that interventions get harder when they involve a large number of transactions and when frontline staff have discretion. Kelkar and Shah built on it by adding stakes and secrecy.

recommendations.item: Ajay Shah on the Dangers of Digital Public Infrastructure (Episode 72 of Brave New World)
recommendations.creator: Brave New World podcast
recommendations.context: Ajay mentions this conversation, based on two chapters of the Kelkar-Shah book, while explaining what a public good really is.
recommendations.reason: It sets out his fundamental objection to the label 'digital public goods': what India builds under that name is generally rival and excludable, so it is not a public good.

recommendations.item: State Building
recommendations.creator: Francis Fukuyama
recommendations.context: Amit recaps the previous episode's use of Fukuyama's scale of state strength and scope.
recommendations.reason: Source of the frame that the ideal state is strong but limited in scope, and that India has the worst of both worlds: a weak state that does too much.

recommendations.item: Understanding the State (Episode 25 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit opens the main discussion with a summary of it, since this episode continues the series.
recommendations.reason: It lays the foundation for this one: the state is coercive, every intervention needs justifying, and Fukuyama's strength-versus-scope lens.

recommendations.item: Public Choice: A Primer
recommendations.creator: Eomonn Butler
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes after Amit raises public choice theory, a field he wants to give a full episode someday.
recommendations.reason: Public choice theory explains why state failure is practically everywhere. It is the needed counterweight to people who cite market failure to justify intervention.

recommendations.item: Amit Varma on Public Choice Theory (mashup of The Seen and the Unseen & The Pragati Podcast)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Show-notes companion to Amit's point that no one talks of state failure.
recommendations.reason: An audio introduction to why the state fails, the half of the story that market-failure talk leaves out.

recommendations.item: Centrally Sponsored Government Schemes (Episode 20 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Pranay Kotasthane
recommendations.context: One of the sources for Amit's argument that government should be as local as possible.
recommendations.reason: It shows how schemes designed in Delhi ignore local needs, a concrete case for subsidiarity.

recommendations.item: South India Would Like to Have a Word (Episode 320 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with RS Nilakantan
recommendations.context: Cited with the Kotasthane episode for the North-South contrast in policy needs.
recommendations.reason: It brings out how different South India's problems are from the North's, while the North's priorities drive national policy.

recommendations.item: How I Reversed My Type 2 Diabetes (Episode 9 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: A quick plug while discussing Kerala's diabetes and obesity problem.
recommendations.reason: Amit's pitch: 'We can conquer diabetes. Yes, we can.'

recommendations.item: Why Freedom Matters (Episode 10 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes for an episode built on freedom as the default.
recommendations.reason: It makes the case for freedom that this episode assumes as its starting point.

recommendations.item: Yes Minister / Yes Prime Minister
recommendations.creator: Jonathan Lynn and Antony Jay
recommendations.context: Amit quotes the series while arguing that the state need not act on every problem.
recommendations.reason: Its line 'we must do something, this is something, therefore we must do this' captures the reflex behind bad interventions.

recommendations.item: Johan Norberg's writings on Sweden
recommendations.creator: Johan Norberg
recommendations.context: Raised when Amit answers the common 'but look at Scandinavia' objection.
recommendations.reason: Norberg shows in detail that the Nordic countries were model free-market economies and got rich before building welfare states.

recommendations.item: Indian Colours
recommendations.context: Ajay explains where his art shirt comes from at the start of the episode.
recommendations.reason: It licenses work from Indian artists, puts it on shirts, mugs and stoles, and pays the artists royalties the way authors are paid for books. Ajay sees it as a novel business model that lets anyone surround themselves with art.

recommendations.item: $800,000 to Zero - The FASCINATING History of DaVinci Resolve
recommendations.creator: Learn Color Grading
recommendations.context: The YouTube video where Amit learned the DaVinci Resolve story he tells.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a great video, a vivid history of how professional tools became free.

recommendations.item: How 32-bit Float Recording Works on the Wireless PRO
recommendations.context: Show-notes link for the new RODE Wireless Pro mics the hosts switched to in this episode.
recommendations.reason: Explains the 32-bit float audio that removes the need to set mic levels while recording.

recommendations.item: The RODE Wireless PRO is NUTS!
recommendations.creator: DLSR Video Shooter
recommendations.context: Show-notes review of the mics the show now uses.
recommendations.reason: A hands-on review of the gear behind the hosts' new freedom to wave their arms about.

recommendations.item: Pune Public Policy Festival (January 19 & 20, 2024)
recommendations.context: The episode's sponsor.
recommendations.reason: Amit's pitch: Pune was once called the Oxford of the East, and public policy discussion has since become centred on Delhi. The festival brings young professionals together with bureaucrats, economists and thinkers around the theme of trade-offs: environment vs growth, growth vs equality, technology vs privacy.

core_ideas.concept: Every State Action Is Justified Violence
core_ideas.explanation: The state is a coercive monopoly on violence. We accept it because we need it to protect our rights. So every proposal that 'the state should do X' must be justified, because it is paid for with coerced taxes. The state is not a cost-free, benevolent beast.
core_ideas.quote: Every time we recommend, you know, that the state should do X or the state should do Y, we should be able to justify it. Because each time we are justifying violence.

core_ideas.explanation: Using Fukuyama's two axes: scope is how much the state does, and strength is how well it does it. The ideal is a state that does few things and does them very well, leaving society to solve its own problems. 'Strong' here means robust democratic systems and enforcement of the rule of law, not a decisive strongman.
core_ideas.quote: India happens to have a weak state that does too much. So it is the worst of both worlds.

core_ideas.concept: Freedom Is the Default; Market Failure Is the Exception
core_ideas.explanation: Economists offer a framework that rises above 'my politics versus yours'. Start from freedom. Intervene only in market failures, where a well-designed intervention can make some people better off without harming anyone, a free lunch. This is not populism or Robin Hood redistribution. It is the opposite of Marx's class warfare, because even a monopolist could sign on to it.
core_ideas.quote: Market failure is a class of problems where there is an analytical and a technical possibility that the correct kind of state intervention is a free lunch because it will make some people in society better off without harming anybody at all.

core_ideas.concept: The Four Kinds of Market Failure
core_ideas.explanation: 1. Market power (monopoly or oligopoly). Natural monopolies should have their prices regulated, not be broken up. 2. Externalities: uncontracted spillovers. Positive ones are vaccines and education, where people underinvest because they ignore the benefit to others. Negative ones are smoking and loudspeakers. 3. Asymmetric information: no consumer can test the purity of a medicine, the hygiene of a restaurant kitchen, or the soundness of a bank. 4. Public goods.
core_ideas.quote: The entire criminal justice system is a negative externality story.

core_ideas.concept: A Public Good Is Non-Rival and Non-Excludable
core_ideas.explanation: A public good is not 'something good for the public'. Non-rival means my use doesn't reduce yours: one woman walking safely doesn't reduce anyone else's safety. Non-excludable means you can't keep anyone out, not even a newborn. Clean air qualifies, which is why Ajay would back taxing to fund 10,000 drones that find and ticket every crop fire in North India. India's so-called 'digital public goods' are generally rival and excludable, so they don't qualify.
core_ideas.quote: Again, the welfareist socialist impulse in India is anything that is good for the people is a public good, and that's just wrong. A public good is something that is non-rival and non-excludable.

core_ideas.concept: Even If You Don't Value Freedom, It's the Path to Prosperity
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay argues as a card-carrying economist. Even a conservative who values order or tradition over freedom should accept the empirical claim: societies that start from freedom and limit the state to workable fixes for market failure get rich.
core_ideas.quote: As a card carrying economist, I'm saying to you that societies flourish when freedom is a baseline and government intervention is limited to the class of market failures where there can be a successful implementation.

core_ideas.concept: Set a High Bar of Proof: Knowledge Is Hard
core_ideas.explanation: Saying 'freedom isn't working' is a utilitarian, consequence-based claim. Amit's worry is that utilitarian, engineering-minded planners assume they know what their interventions will do. So any claim that freedom has failed should face a very high burden of proof, and should not be a convenient excuse to crush freedom.
core_ideas.quote: One of my issues with all utilitarian thinking is that it assumes that knowledge is easy. Knowledge is not easy. Knowledge is very difficult to come by.

core_ideas.explanation: Economics repurposes everyday words as technical terms: market failure, public good, adverse selection, moral hazard. They seem easy to understand when they aren't. 'Market failure' does not mean the shop had only blue cushions when you wanted green. Learn the precise meanings before using them to argue for state action.
core_ideas.quote: This is a bane of economics that in the field of economics we repurpose plain English words.

core_ideas.concept: State Failure Is the Missing Half
core_ideas.explanation: People cite market failure, often wrongly, to justify intervention, but rarely weigh state failure. Public choice theory explains why state failure is practically ubiquitous. Ajay files this under 'implementation constraints'.
core_ideas.quote: People keep talking about market failure, often erroneously, to justify state intervention. No one talks of state failure.

core_ideas.explanation: Market-friendly means open competition. Business-friendly means protecting incumbents, who lobby for tariffs and regulations to keep rivals out, and that hurts consumers. Amit argues genuine monopolies are rare in competitive markets. When you see one, either it has been misdefined or the state is propping it up through cronyism and barriers to entry.
core_ideas.quote: Market friendly means you have competition, anyone can enter. Business friendly means the existing businesses who are there. They want to keep competitors out, which hurts consumers.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit's four-word diagnostic for any social problem. Find the coercion and you usually find the root cause.
core_ideas.quote: Where is the coercion? And where you identify the coercion, often, most of the time, in fact in my case always, you will find that the root of the problem is there.

core_ideas.concept: A Market Failure Doesn't Mean the State Should Act
core_ideas.explanation: A market failure is necessary for intervention but not sufficient. Ask whether the state can actually fix it at low cost. Otherwise you just create a corrupt bureaucracy that pushes private citizens around. Be willing to walk away, and back off when an intervention isn't working.
core_ideas.quote: So living with a market failure is often better than living with a bad state intervention that claims to address that market failure and oftentimes fails to address it.

core_ideas.concept: Four Questions to Judge How Hard an Intervention Is
core_ideas.explanation: A test simple enough for a chat over chai. Pritchett and Woolcock (2004) gave the first two questions, and Kelkar and Shah added the last two. 1. Many transactions? 2. Frontline discretion? Discretion breeds corruption. 3. High stakes? An absent teacher steals about Rs 15,000 a month, but in criminal justice, where liberty is at stake, the pressure to corrupt becomes enormous. 4. Secrecy? A polio drop campaign is easy: many transactions, but no discretion and no identity tracking. Policing, the judiciary, income tax and financial regulation are hard.
core_ideas.quote: In these four zero one numbers, you've got a grip of the essence that some things are easy, some things are hard.

core_ideas.concept: Choose the Least Intrusive Intervention, at the Root Cause
core_ideas.explanation: Most problems can be solved several ways, each with its own winners and losers, so lay out the options and pick the one that intrudes least into people's lives. A rough ranking: touching a body is worse than not touching it, entering a home is worse than knocking, and knocking is worse than not knocking at all. Fixing the root cause is also cheapest: clean the air rather than build hospitals.
core_ideas.quote: So don't build bad roads and then put a trauma center at every highway exit. Build good roads.

core_ideas.explanation: Assign each government function to the lowest level of government that can handle it. Local governments understand local problems, as with Kerala's obesity versus Bihar's malnourishment, in ways a Delhi-designed scheme cannot.
core_ideas.quote: The principle is called the subsidiarity principle. And this is one of the great ideas in economics, which asserts that every problem in government should be placed at the lowest level of government

core_ideas.explanation: State capability takes generations to build. Begin with a few narrow functions and learn the craft of public management through them. Broaden scope later only if society wants to. For India, Ajay thinks the welfare debate is beside the point while the police and judiciary remain unfixed.
core_ideas.quote: For 25 years, for 50 years, we have to learn how to do basics.

core_ideas.concept: Sweden Got Rich Before It Got a Welfare State
core_ideas.explanation: Pointing to Scandinavia misreads it. Those countries have big welfare states but also great individual liberty and easy business entry. They grew rich as free-market economies first, and built welfare once they had the state capacity. Ajay adds that Sweden's cashless economy rests on Swedish levels of rule of law: any single feature of a rich country depends on its wider institutional environment.
core_ideas.quote: While they do have significant welfare states, they also have great individual liberty. They don't get in the way of the citizens. It is so easy to start a business in those countries relative to what it is here.

core_ideas.concept: You Don't Always Have to Do Something
core_ideas.explanation: Resist the Yes Minister reflex of 'we must do something; this is something; therefore we must do this.' Ask whether the action is the right one, and whether it needs doing at all. Government capacity, money and bandwidth are limited, so opportunity cost should push it toward core priorities like the rule of law.
core_ideas.quote: Government has limited capacity, limited money, limited bandwidth. You need to think about what are the core priorities.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay is beaming after the boom arms are gone, and Amit says: 'I have the feeling one day I will disappear and you will be even happier.'

Ajay says Amit 'missed an opportunity to plug a German philosopher.' Amit guesses Kant's categorical imperative. Ajay means Marx: with cheap gear, the 'humble slaves and producers' now own the means of production. Amit lands the pun anyway: 'Who says Immanuel can't? Now Immanuel can.'
Amit's analogy for the new mics: 32-bit float audio is 'like raw for photographs.' It captures all the information, so levels can be fixed afterwards and nothing clips.
Ajay: 'Gentle reader, please Google gutter oil. It will blow your mind.' Amit, who doesn't know what it is: 'I suspect it will blow your guts as well... don't tell me, continue.'
Ajay updates the old fist-and-nose line for the new studio: 'my freedom to move my fist should be limited not just by the absence of the boom arm, but by the proximity of your nose.'

After Ajay keeps casting him as 'the great dictator Amit Bhai', Amit hits back: 'Mr. Shah is a great dictator. Mr. Shah with his authoritarian command over facts. Mr. Shah with his oppression of bad ideas. You are the problem here.'

Amit mocks Ajay's habit of calling everything 'one of the great ideas in economics': 'How many are there? One of the greatest means kitane?' At the sign-off he calls Ajay 'one of the greatest hosts of Everything is Everything', a show with exactly two hosts.
Yes Minister / Yes Prime Minister (Jonathan Lynn and Antony Jay): 'We must do something, this is something, therefore we must do this.'

Marx, 'the great German philosopher who claimed that the history of mankind is a history of class warfare', set up as the opposite of market-failure thinking, which aims to make some better off without hurting anyone.
Pune was once 'the Oxford of the East', an intellectual hub whose centre of gravity shifted to Delhi after independence. Amit hopes the Pune Public Policy Festival helps shift some of it back.
